Chapter 6: The Politics of Victimhood and the Power of Identity
Picture this: a group gathered in a lively community center, voices overlapping as people share stories of struggle and injustice. There’s a real sense of solidarity in the room, but underneath, there’s something else too—a subtle contest. Who’s had it the hardest? Whose pain is the most urgent?
In moments like these, identity becomes more than just how we describe ourselves—it turns into a kind of power. Almost like a ticket to moral authority.
For a lot of people, the language of victimhood feels like a way to finally be heard in a world crowded with noise. Imagine a college freshman, uncertain and searching for where they belong. They find comfort in a campus group that celebrates shared experiences of being marginalized. The group meetings are packed with stories of exclusion and hurt, and our freshman quickly learns: if you want recognition, you first have to claim your wound.
And this isn’t just something that happens in college. In politics, on social media—in so many places—the currency of victimhood gets traded every single day. Leaders and activists frame debates around oppression and privilege, drawing sharp lines between who’s innocent and who’s guilty. The more convincingly someone can show they’ve been wronged, the more their words seem to matter.
Think about a city council meeting. Residents line up, each one sharing their own hardships. The council listens, but all too quickly, the conversation shifts from finding solutions to a kind of contest—who’s suffered the most? And if anyone questions this narrative, they’re met with suspicion, or even accused of lacking empathy.
Over time, chasing victim status almost becomes a ritual. People start to highlight their disadvantages, framing every setback as proof of larger injustice. What happens then? We end up with a culture where grievance gets rewarded, and resilience quietly slips into the background.
Here’s something to pay attention to: as comforting as it can be for some, this focus on identity and victimhood can also drive us apart. Instead of building the bonds of community, we end up with a sort of hierarchy of suffering—where empathy is reserved only for those who fit the story. The promise of unity gets lost in a sea of competing claims.
Most of us don’t even notice how fast this mindset spreads. It shapes the way we talk about issues, the policies we support, and even the leaders we choose. The language of victimhood can be a powerful tool for gaining influence. But it also narrows the space for honest conversation and true understanding.
So, what’s the story behind identity politics? Really, it’s a reminder of our deep need to feel seen and to belong. But when this search for meaning gets filtered through the lens of grievance, the outcome isn’t empowerment—it’s division.
The real challenge? Finding ways to honor each person’s story, without turning pain into a weapon.
